source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 2026): only designer; worked with founders, engineers and ops/marketing; Jan–Apr 2026; Yelo's earlier app (Old page) was live; its home was too crowded, social felt bolted on, dated look; the founders picked among directions A–D; B's layout went forward because booking stays first, combined with A; reaction counts were dropped because they felt tacky and few people would tap them (they came from an earlier iMessage-based version where people reacted to ride requests); feed-card changes were his own judgment; home + feed, search + map, ride options and onboarding are live; vehicles sketched first, then modelled and iterated with Gemini, generated together for consistency; no usage numbers. Takeaways he chose: old habits inform design; booking first, social second; simplifying a crowded home. Follow-up: worked with a PM and ops (not marketing); iOS only.

fields.description: Redesigning a live campus ride-share app: booking first, social second.
fields.intro: Yelo is a student-only campus ride-share. As the only designer at the time, I redesigned its live rider app, from the home screen to ride options and onboarding.
fields.summary: How might we make Yelo’s social side part of getting a ride, without slowing booking down?
fields.overview: I was the only designer at the time, working with the founders, engineers and the wider team. The founders picked the home direction; the feed card changes were my own calls.
fields.impact: The redesign is live: home and feed, search and map, ride options and onboarding.

sections.title: Problem
sections.heading: A crowded home on a live app
content: Yelo’s earlier app was already live. Three things weren’t working on its home:

content.alt: Two iPhones: Yelo’s earlier home with a dark photo header, ticker and hotness scores, and the redesigned home with search first and feed cards for where people are headed, tickets and trending searches
content.caption: Before: the earlier home. After: the redesign.

sections.title: Four directions
sections.heading: Four ways to lay out the home screen
content: My early sketches asked one question: what’s the best way to show that a place is popular?

content.alt: Hand-drawn wireframes of two Yelo home screens and three ways to mark a popular location
content.caption: Early sketches: three ways to mark a popular place.

content: Four of the home layouts I explored became directions A to D:

bullets: **A:** feed first, with search in a bottom sheet.
**C:** the feed as chat bubbles with reactions.
**D:** a ranked list of popular places.

content.alt: Four iPhones showing Yelo home directions: feed first, search first, chat bubbles, ranked list
content.caption: A, B, C and D.

content: The founders picked the direction. V1 mixed B and A:

bullets: **B’s layout:** booking stays first, so search sits at the top.
**A’s live row:** “Someone is searching for a ride…”

**No reaction counts:** they came from an earlier version that ran through iMessage, where we noticed people reacting to each other’s ride requests. But they felt a bit tacky, and we didn’t think many people would tap them.

content.alt: An iPhone showing the Yelo V1 home: search first, a Someone is searching for a ride row, and feed cards without reaction counts
content.caption: V1 home.

sections.title: Feed card
sections.heading: A card that says who and where
content: After V1, I kept changing the feed card. These were my own calls:

bullets: “Someone you may know” became a MUTUAL tag.
Labels for each kind of signal came in one at a time: HEADED TO, then TRENDING SEARCH, then GOT TICKETS.

content.alt: Four iPhones showing the Yelo feed card change: Ride to cards, Headed to cards with initials, a MUTUAL tag, and labelled cards
content.caption: Left to right: V1 to the latest card.

sections.title: Ride options
sections.heading: Three versions of the ride sheet
content: The ride sheet went from Exclusive vs. Shared with a seat stepper, to ETA first, to four named vehicle classes with one tag each.

content.alt: Three iPhones showing Yelo ride sheet versions: Exclusive or Shared with a seat stepper, ETA first, and named vehicle classes with 3D cars
content.caption: Ride sheet versions, left to right.

content: I sketched the vehicles first, then used Gemini to model and iterate on them. I started with one vehicle at a time, then switched to generating them all in one image because it gave more consistent results.

content.alt: Five yellow 3D vehicles in a row: sedan, SUV, golf cart with a flag, van and bus
content.caption: The Yelo fleet.

sections.title: Rest of the app
sections.heading: Sign-up, permissions and the map
content: Sign-up checks student status with a school email, through Google, Microsoft or a one-time pin.

content.alt: Three iPhones: Yelo student sign-up with Google or Microsoft, permissions with a reason for each, and the event map
content.caption: Student sign-up, permissions with a reason for each, and the event map.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: What shipped
content: Home and feed, search and map, ride options and onboarding are live. I don’t have usage numbers.

bullets: **Old habits inform design.** How people used the iMessage version shaped what we kept and what we dropped.
**Booking first, social second.** Social signals only help if they don’t slow down getting a ride.
**Simplify a crowded home.** Redesigning a live app is mostly deciding what to remove.
